entities.name: Winston Churchill
entities.label: Person
entities.summary: Sir Winston Leonard Spencer Churchill (1874–1965) was a British statesman, military officer, and author who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom during World War II (1940–1945) and again from 1951–1955 — widely regarded as the greatest wartime leader of the 20th century and the man who rallied the free world against Nazi tyranny when Britain stood alone. Born at Blenheim Palace to a politically prominent family, he served as a cavalry officer in India, Sudan, and South Africa (where he was captured and escaped during the Boer War, becoming a national hero). His political career spanned six decades: First Lord of the Admiralty (twice), Chancellor of the Exchequer, Home Secretary, and multiple cabinet positions. After a ‘wilderness years’ decade (1929–1939) warning against appeasing Hitler when few would listen, he became Prime Minister on May 10, 1940 — the day Germany invaded France. His wartime speeches (‘We shall fight on the beaches,’ ‘Their finest hour,’ ‘Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few’) are among the most powerful oratory in the English language and sustained British morale during the Blitz, the Battle of Britain, and the darkest days of the war. He forged the Anglo-American alliance with Roosevelt, navigated the complex partnership with Stalin, and helped plan D-Day and the defeat of Nazi Germany. He coined the term ‘Iron Curtain’ in his Fulton speech (1946), defining the Cold War. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature (1953) for his six-volume The Second World War and A History of the English-Speaking Peoples. In a 2002 BBC poll, Britons voted him the Greatest Briton of all time.

entities.label: Person
entities.summary: British Prime Minister (1874–1965) who led the United Kingdom through World War II with defiant speeches and indomitable will. A historian, writer, and Nobel laureate, he rallied Allied resistance against Nazi Germany and shaped the postwar world order.
